title: Position: Academic Conferences are Potentially Facing Denominator Gaming Caused by Fully Automated Scientific Agents
claim: Under a fixed acceptance rate, flooding the pool with junk submissions forces more acceptances and lets borderline legitimate work through.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right flow, shared legend at bottom
description: Two stacked panels with blue titles show the same pipeline: submitted papers on the left, a funnel labeled 'Conference Peer Review: Stable Acceptance Rate α, e.g., α ≈ 25%' in the middle, and accepted or rejected papers on the right. The top panel, 'Traditional Conference Submission Process', has four human-authored paper icons going in. One comes out green with a check mark and three come out red with crosses. The bottom panel, 'Agentic Conference Denominator Gaming', has twelve papers going in: four human-authored and eight robot-marked agent-generated ones. Three come out green and nine come out red. The extra green paper is human-authored. A legend at the bottom explains the human icon, the robot icon (low-quality, in red text), and the green and red document colors. The eye goes first to the blue titles and the green/red outcome grids.
caption: An illustration of the mechanism of Agentic Conference Denominator Gaming. Assume a conference maintains a stable acceptance rate of around 25%. If the denominator increases from 4 to 12, the number of accepted papers must rise from 1 to 3. Without an influx of new high-quality submissions, this mechanism forces the conference to lower its quality threshold, effectively rescuing human-authored papers that were originally at or even below the borderline.
abstract: The implicit policy of maintaining relatively stable acceptance rates at top AI conferences, despite exponentially growing submissions, introduces a critical structural vulnerability. This position paper characterizes a new systemic threat we term Agentic Denominator Gaming, in which a malicious actor deploys AI agents to generate and submit a large volume of superficially plausible but low-quality papers. Crucially, their objective is not the acceptance of low-quality papers, but rather to inflate the submission denominator and overwhelm reviewing capacity. Under a relatively stable acceptance rate, this dilution can systematically increase the publication probability of a small, targeted set of legitimate papers. We analyze the practical feasibility of this threat and its broader consequences, including intensified reviewer burnout, degraded review quality, and the emergence of industrialized automated agent mills. Finally, we propose and evaluate a range of mitigation strategies, and argue that durable protection will require system-level policy and incentive reforms, rather than relying primarily on technical detection alone.
